quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-01.title: Normalizers grow in $p$-groups
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-01.body:
We use: if $D<S$ with $S$ a $p$-group, then $D<N_S(D)$ ("normalizers grow").

**(a)** Let $D=S\cap T$. Since $S\ne T$ and $|S|=|T|$, $D<S$ and $D<T$, so $N_S(D)>D$ and $N_T(D)>D$. Put $N=\mathbf N_G(D)$ and suppose $N$ has a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup $P_0$, so $P_0\trianglelefteq N$ contains every $p$-subgroup of $N$; in particular $N_S(D),N_T(D)\le P_0$. Let $U\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ contain $P_0$. Then
$$U\cap S\supseteq N_S(D)>D,\qquad U\cap T\supseteq N_T(D)>D.$$
If $U\ne S$, then $U\cap S$ is an intersection of two distinct Sylow $p$-subgroups strictly larger than $D$, contradicting maximality; so $U=S$. Likewise $U=T$. Hence $S=T$, a contradiction. So $N$ has more than one Sylow $p$-subgroup.

**(b)** ($\Rightarrow$) Assume distinct Sylow $p$-subgroups intersect trivially, and let $1\ne P$ be a $p$-subgroup with $N=\mathbf N_G(P)$. If $Q_1\ne Q_2$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $N$, then $P\trianglelefteq N$ gives $PQ_i$ a $p$-subgroup of $N$, so $P\le Q_i$. Choose $S_i\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ with $Q_i\le S_i$. If $S_1=S_2=S$, then $S\cap N$ is a $p$-subgroup of $N$ containing the Sylow subgroups $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, so $Q_1=S\cap N=Q_2$, a contradiction. Thus $S_1\ne S_2$ while $S_1\cap S_2\supseteq P\ne1$, contradicting the hypothesis. So $N$ has exactly one Sylow $p$-subgroup.

($\Leftarrow$) Assume the normalizer condition and suppose some distinct $S,T$ have $S\cap T\ne1$. Among all pairs of distinct Sylow $p$-subgroups choose one, $S',T'$, with $S'\cap T'$ maximal; then $S'\cap T'\ne1$ as well (it is at least as large as $S\cap T$). By (a), $\mathbf N_G(S'\cap T')$ has more than one Sylow $p$-subgroup, although $S'\cap T'$ is a nonidentity $p$-subgroup — a contradiction. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-02.title: Primary ideals and the Krull intersection theorem
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-02.body:
"Primary ideal" means a proper ideal $I$ such that $xy\in I$, $x\notin I$ imply $y^k\in I$ for some $k$.

**(a)** $P^n\subseteq P$ gives $\sqrt{P^n}\subseteq\sqrt P=P$. Conversely, if $x\in P$ then $x^n\in P^n$, so $x\in\sqrt{P^n}$. Hence $\sqrt{P^n}=P$.

**(b)** Some maximal ideal exists and is a nonzero prime (as $R$ has a nonzero prime, it is not a field), so $P$ is the unique maximal ideal and the primes of $R$ are exactly $0$ and $P$. Let $I$ be a proper ideal.
- If $I=0$: $0$ is prime in a domain, hence primary.
- If $I\ne0$: $\sqrt I$ is the intersection of the primes containing $I$; the only one is $P$ (since $I\subseteq P$ and $I\not\subseteq0$). So $\sqrt I=P$. In $\bar R=R/I$ the nilradical $P/I$ is the unique prime, hence the unique maximal ideal; so every element of $\bar R$ is a unit or nilpotent. If $xy\in I$ with $x\notin I$, then $\bar y$ is a zero divisor of $\bar R$ (as $\bar x\bar y=0$, $\bar x\ne0$), not a unit, hence nilpotent: $y^k\in I$. So $I$ is primary.

**(c)** Fix $n\ge1$. Since $Q\not\supseteq P$, choose $a\in P\setminus Q$. Let $I=P^n\cap Q$, a proper ideal, primary by hypothesis. Let $q\in Q$. Then $a^nq\in P^n\cap Q=I$. No power of $a^n$ lies in $I$: $(a^n)^j\in I\subseteq Q$ would force $a\in Q$ since $Q$ is prime. By primariness, $q\in I\subseteq P^n$. Hence $Q\subseteq P^n$ for every $n$. (So $P^n\cap Q=Q$: the intersection is never irredundant.)

Therefore $Q\subseteq\bigcap_{n\ge1}P^n$. By the Krull intersection theorem, in a Noetherian domain $\bigcap_n I^n=0$ for every proper ideal $I$; $P$ is proper, so $Q=0$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-03.title: Galois action on the roots
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-03.body:
Since $\operatorname{char}F=0$, $f$ is separable, $E/F$ is Galois, and $G=\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ acts transitively on $\Omega$ ($f$ irreducible). Also $0\notin\Omega$, since an irreducible $f$ of degree $>1$ is not divisible by $X$.

**(a)** $g$ is irreducible with the root $\alpha^m\in E$, and $E/F$ is normal, so $g$ splits in $E$ and its roots are exactly the conjugates $\sigma(\alpha^m)=\sigma(\alpha)^m$, $\sigma\in G$. As $\sigma$ ranges over $G$, $\sigma(\alpha)$ ranges over all of $\Omega$ (transitivity). Hence the set of roots of $g$ is $\{\beta^m\mid\beta\in\Omega\}$.

**(b)** Let $\beta\in\Omega$ and choose $\sigma\in G$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=\beta$. Since $\sigma$ permutes $\Omega$ and fixes $r\in F$, $\sigma(\alpha r)=\beta r\in\Omega$. So $\Omega r\subseteq\Omega$ (the hypothesis transfers from $\alpha$ to every root), and by induction $\beta r^i=(\beta r^{i-1})r\in\Omega$ for all $i\ge0$.

The elements $\alpha r^i$, $i\ge0$, lie in the finite set $\Omega$, so $\alpha r^i=\alpha r^j$ for some $i<j$. As $\alpha\neq0$ (and then $r\ne0$), $r^{j-i}=1$: $r$ is a root of unity.

**(c)** We take $f$ monic (in general the identity holds up to the leading coefficient of $f$). Let $m$ be the order of $r$, so $\langle r\rangle=\{1,r,\dots,r^{m-1}\}$ is the group of all $m$-th roots of unity ($X^m-1$ has at most $m$ roots), and $r\in F$.

*Roots of $g(X^m)$ lie in $\Omega$:* if $g(\gamma^m)=0$ then by (a) $\gamma^m=\beta^m$ for some $\beta\in\Omega$, so $(\gamma/\beta)^m=1$, $\gamma=\beta r^k\in\Omega$ by (b).

*Every $\beta\in\Omega$ is a root of $g(X^m)$:* by (a).

*Separability:* $g$ is separable (characteristic $0$) with nonzero roots $c$ (as $\alpha\ne0$), and each $X^m-c$ with $c\ne0$ has $m$ distinct roots (its derivative $mX^{m-1}$ has only the root $0$); different $c$ give disjoint root sets. So $g(X^m)$, of degree $m\deg g$, has $m\deg g$ distinct roots.

Thus $g(X^m)$ is monic and squarefree with root set exactly $\Omega$, so $g(X^m)=\prod_{\gamma\in\Omega}(X-\gamma)=f(X)$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-04.title: Rank–nullity for the two induced maps
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2007s-04.body:
**(a)** For $x\in V$ define $T(x)\colon V/R\to K$ by $T(x)(y+R)=\langle x,y\rangle$. This is well defined: if $y-y'\in R$ then $\langle x,y-y'\rangle=0$ since $\langle V,R\rangle=0$. It is linear in $y$, so $T(x)\in(V/R)^*$, and $T$ is linear in $x$ by bilinearity. Finally $T(x)=0$ iff $\langle x,y\rangle=0$ for all $y\in V$ iff $x\in L$. So $\ker T=L$.

**(b)** Symmetrically, $T'\colon V\to (V/L)^*$, $T'(y)(x+L)=\langle x,y\rangle$, is well defined and linear with $\ker T'=R$. Let $n=\dim V$. By rank–nullity, using $\dim(V/R)^*=n-\dim R$:
$$n-\dim L=\operatorname{rank}T\le n-\dim R,\qquad n-\dim R=\operatorname{rank}T'\le n-\dim L.$$
Hence $\dim R\le\dim L\le\dim R$, so $\dim L=\dim R$. Then $\operatorname{rank}T=n-\dim L=n-\dim R=\dim(V/R)^*$, so $T$ is surjective. ∎
